description: THE PERIHELION INITIATIVE. A collective of curious minds united by a passion for technology and innovation. We explore the unknown, challenge limits, and turn ideas into reality through creativity, collaboration, and code. You don't have to be the best to begin, just willing to learn and grow. Join us and make our next breakthrough extraordinary!
summary:
Perihelion Earth Jukebox is an innovative web platform that transforms Earth observation and climate data into an interactive audiovisual experience. By converting scientific measurements into sound, users can hear environmental patterns and changes that are often difficult to understand through traditional charts alone.

Developed by The Perihelion Initiative, the project reimagines science communication through data sonification, making complex Earth science information more engaging, accessible, and memorable. Our solution demonstrates how technology and creativity can work together to inspire greater awareness of our changing planet, by turning complex NASA Earth data into an accessible, multi-sensory soundscape for blind and low-vision communities.
details:
What does it do, and how does it work?

Perihelion Earth Jukebox turns NASA Earth Information Center (EIC) visualizations into music, so people can hear how the planet is changing instead of only looking at it. A visitor picks a “record”, presses play, and listens. Calm, open sounds mean a steady picture. As the picture gets brighter, busier and changes faster, the music gets faster, tenser and more intense.

We built five records from EIC visualizations: Night Lights, global CO₂, Lightning from the ISS, Ocean Currents and Forest Height. Each one has its own sound:

  • Night Lights: soft bell notes for cities switching on.
  • CO₂: a heavy, low drone with a heartbeat.
  • Lightning: thunder built from many parts, with sharp cracks, rolling rumbles and distant echoes.
  • Ocean: slow, flowing tones with wave sounds.
  • Forest Height: warm strings and a flute-like melody.

How it works:

  • Frames. Each NASA visualization is sampled into 48 still frames.
  • Computer vision. Python (OpenCV and NumPy) measures each frame's brightness, active coverage, frame-to-frame change, and spatial distributions across 8 west-to-east and 8 north-to-south strips.
  • JSON feature export. Those measurements are exported into a structured JSON file with per-frame values, tension scores, and scale labels.
  • Place becomes sound. West-to-east strips drive melody pitch and left-to-right stereo panning, while the brightest north-to-south strip selects the chord root.
  • JSON-driven sound generation. The sound is generated directly from the JSON file, using its frame-by-frame feature and timeline fields (tension, scale, and spatial bands) to drive the audio.

What are the benefits?

  • Access for blind and low-vision communities. NASA’s visualizations are visual. Sound opens them to people who can’t see them, and to anyone who learns better by listening.
  • Easier to understand than a chart. Listeners can hear change, speed and intensity directly, without reading axes.
  • Simple to use. Pick a record and press play. Our site has: plain-language descriptions, screen-reader support, high contrast.
  • Every sound has a reason. The sound follows written rules, so it can be explained and trusted.
  • Free and open. It runs in a web browser with no installation.

What is the intended impact?

We want more people to feel and understand how the planet is changing, and to make Earth science something everyone can experience, including communities that are usually left out. We hope to inspire curiosity and awareness, and to show teachers, students and scientists that sonification is a practical way to share science.

Tools, languages, hardware and software

  • Python & JSON: For image analysis, feature extraction, and audio synthesis. The Python engine generates the .mp3 audio files and .json timeline data.
  • React & JavaScript XML(JSX): For building the user interface. We use JSX to structure the components, manage state, and sync the visuals.
  • JavaScript: For the browser-based playback engine, reading the JSON timeline, and synchronizing the frames to the audio.
  • CSS & Tailwind CSS: For styling, 3D transforms, and the immersive Jukebox animations.
  • Vite: For fast bundling and local development.
  • Vercel: For hosting and deployment.
  • Ordinary Hardware: Runs entirely on ordinary laptops. No special hardware required.

How is it creative?

  • One tension score ties everything together: the scale, the tempo and the look of the screen.
  • Every record has its own instruments. The sounds are not a single recipe applied to every dataset.
  • The thunder is built the way real thunder forms. The lightning track models a jagged lightning channel whose sound reaches the listener piece by piece, so crack, rumble and echoes arrive at different moments.
  • Geography you can hear. Longitude becomes stereo position, and the brightest latitude picks the harmony.
  • Music, not noise. Raw pixel-to-pitch sounds chaotic, so we pass everything through musical scales. It sounds pleasant while it still follows the data.

What factors did we consider?

  • Accessibility first. The experience is designed to work with human assistance, without requiring the user to look at the screen.
  • Honesty about the data. Our sounds come from measurements of NASA’s visualizations (brightness, coverage and change in the images), not from the original science datasets. Some changes in the sound come from camera motion, such as a rotating globe or a zoom panel appearing. Sonification is a companion to the visuals, not a replacement.
  • Musicality and accuracy together. We balanced a pleasant sound against faithfulness to the picture.
  • Reliability. Our data is stored locally and we pre-rendered backup audio, so a demo doesn’t depend on a live internet connection.
  • Simplicity for the public. We used plain language and a simple interface so people of any background can use it.
  • Reproducibility. Our tools can be re-run on other NASA visualizations.
  • Credit. Every visualization is credited to NASA’s Scientific Visualization Studio and the Earth Information Center.
